facts.text: The male wears a striking black-and-white outfit, with a black 'hood' over the head and neck and a white stripe along the shoulder.
facts.quote: The male has a distinctive pied coloration, with a black head and neck ("hood") and a white stripe along its shoulder.

facts.text: The female is far plainer than the male, being grey-brown above with a pale grey throat and paler underparts.
facts.quote: The female is an undistinguished grey-brown above, with a pale grey throat and paler underneath, and dark brown wings and white wing bars.

facts.text: Juveniles moult through several plumages over a three-year period before gaining adult colouring.
facts.quote: Juveniles transition through several moults over a 3-year period.

facts.text: The male's square-ended tail shows distinctive white panels that are clearly visible in flight.
facts.quote: the square-ended tail is white tipped underneath with distinctive white panels on the dorsal side, each of which are clearly visible in flight.

facts.text: Though normally quiet, hooded robins call in the early morning, and pairs or small groups are often seen together.
facts.quote: Though normally a quiet bird, male birds call in the early morning.

facts.text: Hooded robins catch invertebrates by pouncing on them from an exposed perch close to the ground.
facts.quote: catch invertebrates by pouncing on them from an exposed perch close to the ground.

facts.text: Both sexes may tumble along the ground feigning injury to distract predators approaching their nest.
facts.quote: Injury-feigning displays, including tumbling along the ground, have been observed in both sexes, to distract potential predators and humans that encroach upon occupied nests.

facts.text: The hooded robin prefers dry open forests with acacias and eucalypts, using shrubs as perches close to the ground.
facts.quote: The hooded robin shows a preference for dry open forests, combining acacia and eucalypts with shrubs that offer perching positions relatively close to the ground.
